title: Probability, Bayes & Distributions
html:
ML models are statistical models. A handful of probability ideas — conditional probability, Bayes' rule, common distributions, the central limit theorem and maximum likelihood — explain most of what they do.

Rules you use constantly

RuleFormula
Conditional probabilityP(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)
IndependenceP(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B) ⇔ P(A | B) = P(A)
AdditionP(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
Total probabilityP(B) = Σᵢ P(B | Aᵢ)·P(Aᵢ) for a partition A₁, A₂, …
Bayes' ruleP(A | B) = P(B | A)·P(A) / P(B)

Bayes' rule and the base-rate fallacy

A disease affects 1% of people. A test catches 99% of cases (sensitivity) and correctly clears 95% of healthy people (specificity). Given a positive test, how likely is the disease?

Most positives come from the huge healthy group. This is exactly why precision collapses on rare classes even for an accurate classifier — and why the base rate must be part of any threshold decision.

Central limit theorem

Central limit theorem — for independent, identically distributed observations with finite variance σ², the distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n as n grows — whatever the shape of the original distribution.

standard error of the mean = σ / √n
Watch out

The CLT is about means (and sums), not the data: it does not make your features normal. It needs finite variance (it fails for the Cauchy distribution) and independent observations; how large n must be depends on the skew — 30 is folklore, not a law.

The law of large numbers is the simpler cousin: sample averages converge to the expected value. Together they justify confidence intervals, A/B tests and cross-validation averages.

Maximum likelihood — where loss functions come from

Maximum likelihood estimation picks the parameters under which the observed data is most probable. Two famous consequences: assuming Gaussian noise, maximising the likelihood of a regression model is exactly minimising squared error; assuming Bernoulli labels, it is exactly minimising log-loss (logistic regression).

What is Bayes' theorem and why does it matter in ML?

P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B): it updates a prior belief with evidence. It underlies Naive Bayes, Bayesian inference and the base-rate reasoning behind precision on rare classes — a 99%-sensitive test for a 1%-prevalence disease still gives mostly false positives.

State the central limit theorem.

For i.i.d. samples with finite variance, the sampling distribution of the mean tends to a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n as n grows, regardless of the population's shape. It justifies normal-based confidence intervals and tests for means and proportions.

Why divide by n − 1 for the sample variance?

Deviations are measured from the sample mean, which is itself fitted to the data, so they are on average too small; dividing by n − 1 (one degree of freedom used by the mean) makes the variance estimate unbiased.
